conditional-statements.why: A conditional statement says 'if P then Q'. Its converse swaps the parts, its inverse negates both, and its contrapositive does both. Only the contrapositive is guaranteed to share the original's truth value — and mixing up the converse with the original is among the commonest reasoning errors in everyday life.
traps: 'All dogs are mammals' is true, but 'all mammals are dogs' is not. A true statement does not guarantee a true converse.
Proving the contrapositive proves the original, which is sometimes far easier.

code.note: A programming condition 'if p then q' is false in exactly one case: p true and q false. The contrapositive, if not q then not p, has the same truth table.

deductive-reasoning.why: Deductive reasoning chains established facts to a conclusion that *must* follow. Three patterns are valid: modus ponens (the condition holds, so the result holds), modus tollens (the result fails, so the condition failed) and syllogism (chain two conditionals). One pattern that looks valid is not: affirming the consequent.
traps: From 'if P then Q' and Q you cannot conclude P. Something else may also produce Q.
A valid argument can still have a false conclusion if a premise is false. Validity is about the form, not the facts.

two-column-proof.why: A proof is a chain of statements each justified by a reason: a given, a definition, a property, a postulate or a theorem already proved. The two-column layout makes that discipline visible, because every line has to say why it is allowed.
traps: 'It looks true in the diagram' is never a reason. Diagrams suggest; reasons prove.
Each line may use only what came before it. Quoting something you have not yet established is circular.

counterexamples.why: A general claim can be destroyed by a single counterexample, however many examples agree with it. A counterexample has to meet the claim's conditions and still break its conclusion. The expression ~n^{2} + n + 41~ is prime for every ~n~ from 0 to 39, and fails at 40 — forty agreeing examples proved nothing.
traps: Examples can support a claim but never prove it. One failure disproves it.
A counterexample must satisfy the *conditions* of the claim. A case that does not meet the condition does not count.
